name: Tô
subtitle: Tô (sagbo in the Centre-Nord booklet) is a firm cooked paste of millet or sorghum flour; maize tô is also eaten.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A dish of millet or sorghum flour, described in a Burkinabè research institute recipe booklet under the name tô (sagbo).

facts.label: Preparation of the grain
facts.value: Sorghum grains are soaked for 12 hours, then washed, picked over and drained before grinding.

facts.label: How it is cooked
facts.value: The fine flour is split three quarters to one quarter; the small part is mixed with water to make a 'flour milk'.

facts.label: Cooking liquid
facts.value: In this version the cooking liquid is an infusion of roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa) petals soaked in hot water for 2 hours, which is brought to the boil before the flour milk is added.

facts.label: Finishing
facts.value: The larger part of the flour is added gradually while working it with a spatula.

facts.label: Serving
facts.value: Served with a ladle in small balls.

facts.label: Eaten with
facts.value: A sauce of sorrel, jute, amaranth, spinach or okra leaves, or thinned in water, milk or yoghurt.

facts.label: In restaurants
facts.value: In a Ouagadougou restaurant serving local food, diners ate maize tô with koumvando (African eggplant leaves).

facts.label: Change
facts.value: Burkinabè city dwellers are increasingly fond of traditional dishes long confined to rural areas.

parts.text: Tô (sagbo in the Centre-Nord booklet) is a firm cooked paste of millet or sorghum flour; maize tô is also eaten. The sifted flour is split into a small part, mixed with water into a 'flour milk' and boiled, and a larger part, worked in gradually with a spatula until the paste is cooked and supple.

It is served with a ladle in small balls and eaten with a sauce such as sorrel, jute (corète), amaranth or okra, or thinned with water, milk or yoghurt. City dwellers are increasingly eating traditional dishes such as tô, long associated with rural areas.

gaps: The description is summarised from the sources listed here and should be read against them.

Not found in a readable source: The IRSAT/CNRST booklet gives the full method but only proportions (3/4 and 1/4 of the flour, water 'idem'), not quantities, so it was not recorded as a recipe. No other complete recipe from an acceptable source was found.
